hints: Focus on the three separate rules, protons come from the bottom number, neutrons are mass minus protons, and electrons change with charge.
Try the fluoride ion first, it has 9 protons, 10 neutrons and 10 electrons, so two of the numbers match.
Now repeat that same check for the sodium ion and see if its proton, neutron and electron counts give you three distinct values.
walkthrough:
**Recall what each number tells you**

Great start, let us get the rules clear. The bottom number is the atomic number, so that is protons. The top number is mass number, so neutrons = mass - protons.

$$\text{neutrons} = \text{mass number} - \text{atomic number}$$

**Adjust electrons for charge**

For a neutral atom, electrons = protons. For ions, add electrons for each negative charge and subtract electrons for each positive charge.

$$\text{electrons} = \text{protons} - \text{ion charge}$$

**Pick the all-different one**

Only $^{23}_{11}\text{Na}^{+}$ has three different numbers, 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 10 electrons. The others all have a repeated pair.

options.A: Incorrect. For $^{19}_{9}\text{F}^{-}$, protons = 9, neutrons = 10, electrons = 10. Neutrons and electrons are the same, so not all different.
options.B: Correct. For $^{23}_{11}\text{Na}^{+}$, protons = 11, neutrons = 12, electrons = 10. All three numbers, 11, 12 and 10, are different.
options.C: Incorrect. For $^{31}_{15}\text{P}$ (neutral atom), protons = 15, neutrons = 16, electrons = 15. Protons and electrons are equal, a common trap if you forget neutral atoms have equal p and e.
options.D: Incorrect. For $^{32}_{16}\text{S}^{2-}$, protons = 16, neutrons = 16, electrons = 18. Protons and neutrons are the same, so not all different.
